<explanation>
1. Project Type and Purpose  
   - This is a full-stack LLM gateway and AI asset management system ("New API")  
   - Frontends: a React/Vite SPA under **web/** and an Electron desktop client under **electron/**  
   - Backend: a Go-based HTTP API server (entry point **main.go**), using Gin for routing, layered into routers, middleware, controllers, services, models, and common utilities  
   - Core purpose: receive user requests, enforce auth/quotas, route to downstream LLMs (OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, etc.), perform format conversions, billing, caching, analytics, and persist data  

2. File Structure & Architectural Insights  
   - Top-level “layers”:  
     • **router/** – API endpoints grouping (api, relay, web, dashboard)  
     • **middleware/** – request preprocessing (auth, rate-limit, logging, CORS, etc.)  
     • **controller/** – HTTP handlers implementing business flows  
     • **service/** – core business logic, external calls, billing, caching  
     • **model/** + **common/database.go** – ORM/data objects and DB access  
     • **relay/** – adapter implementations for each external LLM provider, organized by channel  
     • **oauth/** – OAuth provider registry and handling  
     • **pkg/** – reusable libraries (cachex, ionet)  
     • **setting/** – runtime configuration definitions (rate limits, quotas, payment, model settings)  
     • **types/** + **dto/** – algebraic types, request/response schemas  
     • **web/** + **electron/** – two UIs consuming the same HTTP API  
     • **bin/**, **Dockerfile**, **docker-compose.yml** – build & deployment scripts  
   - External dependencies: MySQL/PostgreSQL or SQLite, Redis cache, Pyroscope for profiling, multiple third-party LLMs via HTTP/gRPC  

3. How to Draw an Accurate System Diagram  
   a. Main Components  
     • Client layer: Web SPA (React/Vite) & Electron desktop app  
     • API Gateway: Go HTTP server (Gin router + middleware layer)  
     • Business Logic layer: Controllers → Services → Relay adapters  
     • Data Layer: SQL database (MySQL/Postgres/SQLite) + Redis cache  
     • External Services: OpenAI, Claude, Google Gemini, Midjourney-Proxy, Payment gateways (Stripe, EPay), OAuth providers (Discord, GitHub, LinuxDO, OIDC)  
     • Observability: Pyroscope, built-in pprof, system monitor  
     • Deployment & Orchestration: Docker, Docker Compose, optional BaoTa panel  

   b. Relationships & Data Flow  
     1. User → Web/Electron → HTTPS → API Gateway  
     2. Gateway applies Middleware (auth, rate limit, logging)  
     3. Router delegates to Controllers  
     4. Controllers invoke Service methods  
     5. Services:  
        – Read/write to SQL DB via model/common/db  
        – Read/write to Redis cache  
        – Call external relay adapters (in **relay/**) to fetch or send LLM requests/responses  
        – Perform billing, quotas, format conversions  
     6. Service returns data to Controller → serialized to DTO → HTTP response → back to UI  
     7. For streaming APIs (chat), streaming responses handled by Gateway → SSE/WebSocket to client  

   c. Architectural Patterns & Principles  
     • Layered architecture (Presentation → API → Business → Data)  
     • Adapter pattern for each LLM provider (plug-and-play in **relay/**)  
     • Dependency injection of settings and common utilities  
     • Config-driven behavior using **setting/** and environment variables  
     • Separation of concerns: controllers orchestrate, services execute, models persist  

   d. Key Technologies & Frameworks  
     • Go + Gin (backend)  
     • React + Vite + Tailwind CSS (web frontend)  
     • Electron (desktop client)  
     • MySQL/Postgres/SQLite + GORM (or raw SQL)  
     • Redis (cache & rate limiting)  
     • Docker & Docker Compose  

4. Tailoring the Diagram for This Full-Stack Application  
   - Clearly distinguish two client types (web vs. Electron) both hitting the same API Gateway  
   - Emphasize the API Gateway’s middleware chain before hitting Controllers  
   - Show Controllers → Services → Relay adapters calling out to external AI services  
   - Highlight the persistence tier (Database + Redis)  
   - Include configuration & observability sidecars (Pyroscope, environment variable store)  
   - Illustrate deployment stack: Docker container(s), volumes (/data for SQLite), optional multi-machine concerns (shared Redis, SESSION_SECRET)  

5. Diagramming Guidelines  
   - Use boxes for each layer/component group (Clients, Gateway, Business, Data, External)  
   - Label each box (e.g., “Auth Middleware”, “Controllers”, “Billing Service”, “Relay-OpenAI Adapter”)  
   - Draw directional arrows to show request/response flows (e.g., UI → HTTP → Middleware → Controller → Service → DB or LLM → back)  
   - Color-code by layer:  
     • Blue for frontend clients  
     • Green for API Gateway & middleware  
     • Orange for business services/relay adapters  
     • Gray for data stores  
     • Purple for external systems (LLMs, OAuth, payment)  
   - Use different shapes:  
     • Cylinders for databases/Redis  
     • Clouds for external services  
     • Rectangles for code modules/layers  

6. Detail & Completeness  
   - Include all critical elements: web + electron, middleware chain, router, controllers, services, relay adapters, DB, cache, external LLMs, payment/OAuth providers, deployment containers  
   - Don’t clutter with every single Go package—group by layer or function (e.g., “relay/*” as one box with sub-labels for major providers)  
   - Ensure arrows indicate synchronous vs. asynchronous calls (solid vs. dashed lines)  
   - Annotate any special flows (streaming chat via WebSocket/SSE, migration scripts under **bin/**)  

By following these steps and focusing on the layered interactions and external integrations, you will produce a clear, detailed system design diagram that accurately reflects the New API architecture.
